h: Gardens, Chapels and the Coast Road West
p: The Welsh Mountain Zoo's hillside location gives it a character you don't get in flat parks, but it also means a bit of planning goes a long way. Comfortable footwear is a must, and if you're bringing a pushchair, be ready for some uphill pushing. Many families find it easiest to work their way up early in the day when everyone's fresh, then enjoy a more relaxed downhill amble later on.

Look out for the talks and feeding times throughout the day, especially at the sea lion pool, which is often a highlight for younger visitors. The zoo's woodland and gardens are worth slowing down for too, as there's plenty of nature beyond the enclosures. A packed lunch with a view of the bay is hard to beat on a sunny day.

For something different nearby, head to Rhos-on-Sea, just along the coast, where the tiny St Trillo's Chapel sits right on the seafront. It's a tiny stone building with room for only a handful of people, and a properly quirky spot to visit. Eirias Park in Colwyn Bay has wide open spaces, play areas and sports facilities, ideal for a run-around before or after the zoo.

Garden lovers should head inland to Bodnant Garden in the Conwy Valley, a National Trust treasure famed for its laburnum arch, which turns into a tunnel of golden flowers in late spring. It's a lovely contrast to a day spent among the animals.

If you'd rather leave the car at home, Colwyn Bay station sits on the North Wales Coast line, so a train trip is perfectly doable. Just be warned that the zoo is up a steep hill from the town, so save some energy for the climb.
